item.title: When Is Calling Out Bias Actually Effective?
item.description:
Bias

When Is Calling Out Bias Actually Effective?

Avoid negative side effects by discerning when to call out bias as an ally.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Calling out bias is one of the common prototypes of allyship.
  • When leaders call out bias, it can elicit strong, sometimes dysfunctional reactions.
  • Calling out bias is a powerful, sharp tool; refrain from taking it lightly or overusing it.
Calling out bias is a powerful, sharp tool; refrain from using it to vent your emotions.
Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

Calling out bias, a form of allyship, involves labeling a biased action (e.g., "That is sexist!") and pointing it out as unacceptable ("That’s not OK!"). It is often considered essential to ending discrimination. Calling out can educate a colleague about their biases and reduce future instances of biased behavior. Allies who call out bias are often upheld as courageous fighters who combat injustice.

But is calling out the most effective form of allyship? My team's years of scientific research using a variety of experiments, surveys, and interviews with thousands of leaders and employees paints a nuanced picture. Sometimes, calling out bias can cause unintended harm to the marginalized people allies are trying to support, to the allies themselves, as well as to their organization’s culture. If we aren’t careful and calling out is the first tool we reach for, we risk overusing it, and this has limited effectiveness in improving inclusive behaviors in the long term. Instead, it may breed guilt, shame, polarization, and hostility.

Calling Out Feels Heroic—That’s Part of the Problem

Calling out can sometimes appear uncannily similar to saviorism, which matches the stereotype and patriarchal narrative of a powerful and courageous hero fighting injustice. Yet our research shows that calling out an individual’s bias is no more effective than many other non-confrontational forms of allyship.

Although experiencing righteous indignation is natural in the face of injustice, don’t jump into calling out bias because you are enraged or want to vent your own emotions. Be mindful about how you are supporting the victim, so you don’t inadvertently do more harm than good.

Plus, some of us may—knowingly or unknowingly—be motivated to call out bias for our own personal gain, especially if allies are revered in our environment. Performative allyship not only harms victims, but also fuels others’ cynicism toward equity and inclusion efforts.

Calling Out May Be a Poster Child of Allyship, But Few Do It—and That Might Be Wise

Even though calling out is seen as the poster child of what allyship looks like, our research shows that many people freeze when they believe they need to call out bias to be a good ally. For instance, even among men who strongly value gender equity, only a third can see themselves calling out discrimination. Further, they believe that calling out bias is justified only when a transgression is particularly egregious in the context of their organization. In contrast, over 90%, that is, most men who value gender equity, are willing to engage in non-confrontational forms of allyship - which, importantly, our research shows are even more effective in supporting victims of injustice. Besides, for those who are not skilled at calling out bias effectively, utilizing non-confrontational approaches might carry the fewest unintended negative side-effects.

article continues after advertisement

When Leaders Call Out Bias, It Elicits Strong Reactions

Studies on reward and punishment show that when criticism feels harsh and punitive, it evokes defensiveness, shame, withdrawal, and surface-level compliance rather than long-term learning. And it hurts relationships. We can expect similar reactions if being called out feels harsh and punitive.

This appears to be the case even when people observe leaders who call out others' bias. Our research shows that they tend to have one of two strong reactions. While some observers voice their own support for the victim of bias on whose behalf their leader called out bias, others lash out and blame the victim, even though they had nothing to do with the leader-ally's decision to call out. Further, when leaders call out bias, some observers intensify their support for the transgressor and attempt to justify or condone their biased behavior. The leader-allies are also likely to be criticized for ‘going too far’. Ultimately, after this kind of pushback, many well-intentioned leaders and employees—including marginalized ones—may hesitate to speak up about injustice in the future.

As a leader or manager, consider the kinds of allyship behaviors you want to model for the observers in your environment. How observers perceive different allyship interventions is a relevant consideration for leaders who want to normalize and scale up allyship.

Toxic Environments Breed Toxic Call-Outs

Ironically, in toxic environments, where the urge to indignantly call out bias might be the strongest, it might carry the most dysfunctional consequences. So it makes sense that, as my team's research shows, marginalized groups—particularly in toxic environments—prefer that allies prioritize advancing and promoting them over calling out individual transgressors on their behalf. So before calling out, it might be useful to first ask yourself: Can my team's or organization’s culture handle bias call-outs productively by learning, forgiving, and establishing better behavior patterns rather than getting defensive, lashing out at the victim, or justifying the transgressor? Will calling out one person's behavior be effective if a particular instance of bias is part of an organization-wide pattern? Or would it be more useful to address this pattern through system-wide policy or culture change? Then decide whether a different approach to allyship may be more effective.

When Is It Useful to Call Out Bias?

If a transgression is egregious and urgent. Egregious transgressions unquestionably call for bold action to create safety. Observers are also less likely to justify or condone egregious behaviors and more likely to support the victim and ally. Importantly, when leaders do not call out egregious behaviors, they normalize them and lose the trust of their employees.

article continues after advertisement

When the “transgressor” is an organizational structure or system. When we call out individuals’ bias, we risk intensifying backlash and polarization. But calling out biased systems and structures in a de-personalized manner points to problems that leaders and employees can come together to address through values-driven action. Of note, setting realistic goals that can be accomplished in a given period of time is essential to unifying people and avoiding overwhelm or defensiveness.

If the victim wants you to confront on their behalf. Confronting without first having a victim’s consent can pose problems. Because allies have different lived experiences than marginalized groups, allies may be blind to the impact of their confrontation. And some people may simply prefer not to be dragged into the spotlight as victims of bias because it may not be the right time for them. If you see something questionable, talk to the person you believe is affected. Asking for their consent and input before intervening can alert you to underlying toxic dynamics and prevent harm.

In Closing

Allyship should not be considered a binary choice between calling out bias or being silent. Rather, a wealth of research suggests that leaders should consider calling out bias as one tool within a broader repertoire of allyship strategies such as pivoting to loudly celebrate marginalized members' strengths. Especially during times of hostility and polarization, leaders who respond to discrimination in ways that maximize inclusion and minimize adverse effects will be most successful.

item.title: Confidence, Vulnerability, Biology: A Crisis Young Men Face
item.description:
Confidence

Confidence, Vulnerability, Biology: A Crisis Young Men Face

Why belonging, purpose, and healthy masculinity matter more than ever.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy masculinity channels ambition, anger, and drive with wisdom.
  • Young men are searching for belonging—not simply confidence.
  • Vulnerability and strength are complementary, not opposing qualities.

Young men in the United States appear to be facing a growing crisis of loneliness, uncertainty, and disconnection.

Gallup data collected in 2023 and 2024 found that 25% of U.S. men ages 15 to 34 reported feeling lonely "a lot" during the previous day, compared with 18% of women the same age (Dugan, 2025). Men are also more likely to misuse drugs, and male overdose mortality rates remain substantially higher than female rates (NIDA, 2020, 2023). The disparity is even more striking in suicide: in 2024, the age-adjusted U.S. suicide rate was 22.2 deaths per 100,000 males compared with 5.6 for females (CDC, 2026a).

These statistics came to mind while watching a CNN segment about the rise of "man camps"—boot-camp-style programs promising greater confidence, practical skills, self-awareness, and dating success.

Their popularity may reflect something deeper than dating anxiety. Many young men seem to be asking not only "How do I become more confident?" but also "Where do I belong, and what does it mean to become a man?"

Doubt and Disconnection

NYU professor Scott Galloway has argued that many young men are increasingly falling behind in education, employment, friendship, and romantic relationships.

Self-doubt may both result from and reinforce this pattern. Academic struggles can erode confidence. Limited economic opportunity may delay independence. Romantic rejection can deepen feelings of inadequacy. Over time, these experiences can lead some young men to withdraw from precisely the experiences that build resilience, competence, and connection.

Educational trends illustrate the challenge. In 2022, 57% of male high school graduates immediately enrolled in college, compared with 66% of female graduates (NCES, 2024a). Among students entering four-year institutions, men also graduated at lower rates (NCES, 2024b).

College is not the only path to adulthood or success. But when young men disengage from education or vocational training, they may also lose important sources of structure, identity, community, and opportunity.

The dating landscape reflects a similar pattern. Pew Research Center found that 63% of men under 30 identified as single, compared with 34% of women (Brown, 2023). While demographic factors partly explain the difference, the findings suggest many young men are struggling to establish lasting romantic relationships.

Without meaningful work, close friendships, or intimate relationships, some retreat into pornography, video games, grievance-based online communities, or endless digital distraction. None of these pursuits is inherently harmful, and online communities can provide genuine connection. The problem arises when virtual engagement consistently replaces face-to-face relationships, purposeful activity, and the willingness to risk failure or rejection.

The issue, then, may not simply be confidence. Many young men appear uncertain about where they belong, what they can contribute, and what adulthood should look like.

The Double Bind of Male Vulnerability

One challenge is the conflicting messages boys receive about vulnerability.

They are increasingly encouraged to be emotionally aware, expressive, and compassionate. Yet they also learn that showing too much vulnerability can make them appear weak or less masculine.

This creates a double bind.

Can I be emotionally open and still be respected? Will people admire my sensitivity—or lose respect for me?

I saw this tension with my own son after he was bullied. My spouse and I encouraged calm, respectful responses. He rejected some of our suggestions because they felt "too soft" and, in his view, would invite more bullying. His reaction captured an important reality: advice that sounds wise to adults may feel socially costly in the environments boys actually inhabit.

Healthy vulnerability does not mean emotional oversharing or abandoning strength. It means recognizing emotions, expressing them appropriately, asking for help when needed, and remaining engaged despite the possibility of rejection.

Strength and vulnerability are not opposites. In many ways, to permit oneself to be vulnerable requires a certain type of strength.

Our task is not simply to encourage boys to express emotions, but to create families, schools, workplaces, friendships, and intimate relationships where emotional honesty is genuinely respected rather than merely praised in theory.

Positive male role models matter here. Fathers, coaches, teachers, mentors, counselors, and community leaders can demonstrate that courage includes acknowledging fear, grief, uncertainty, and disappointment without surrendering dignity or self-respect.

Biology Is Not Destiny

A second issue involves biology.

During puberty, testosterone contributes to physical changes including increased muscle mass, sexual maturation, libido, and greater physical strength (Nassar & Leslie, 2023). Recognizing these influences does not reduce complex human behavior to hormones or excuse harmful conduct.

Human behavior emerges through the interaction of biology, temperament, family, culture, trauma, peers, opportunity, and personal choice.

Still, avoiding conversations about physical strength, competition, sexuality, anger, or status does boys few favors. When traits commonly associated with masculinity are discussed only as problems to manage, some young men may conclude that an important part of themselves is inherently dangerous or shameful.

Certainly, aggression, coercion, and reckless risk-taking deserve firm limits. But guiding these impulses does not require shaming boys for experiencing ambition, physical energy, competitiveness, anger, or sexual desire.

Instead, the goal is integration.

Physical energy can become athletics, skilled trades, exploration, or service. Competitiveness can fuel mastery and perseverance. Assertiveness can coexist with empathy. Sexual desire can be integrated with patience, mutual respect, and consent. Anger can become information rather than instruction.

The question is not how to eliminate these capacities, but how to help young men understand and govern them wisely.

Boys need adults willing to speak honestly about strength, sexuality, competition, rejection, responsibility, and emotional pain—without either glorifying or condemning them. They also need meaningful opportunities to take risks, build competence, contribute to others, and experience earned success.

A Broader Definition of Manhood

The struggles facing young men cannot be explained by any single cause. Economic uncertainty, educational disengagement, changing gender roles, digital isolation, family disruption, and the weakening of community institutions likely all contribute.

But any meaningful response must help young men answer two enduring questions:

How can I be emotionally open without losing my sense of dignity?

How can I channel strength, ambition, sexuality, competitiveness, and anger in ways that benefit both myself and others?

Young men do not need a return to rigid, emotionally restrictive models of masculinity. Nor do they need to be told that masculinity itself is the problem.

They need a broader and more humane vision of manhood—one that makes room for strength and tenderness, ambition and service, independence and connection, courage and compassion.

The goal is not to make young men less masculine. It is to help them discover forms of masculinity that are authentic, responsible, emotionally mature, and deeply connected to the well-being of others.

item.title: Never Alone, Never Seen
item.description:
Loneliness

Never Alone, Never Seen

The loneliness of Friday couscous.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Moroccan participants describe connection as obligatory; being sociable is seen as marker of good character.
  • Because people are rarely physically alone, loneliness becomes hard to name, claim, or legitimize.
  • Communal rituals like Friday couscous can amplify loneliness for those who already feel unseen.
  • Faith offers real comfort; professional help remains distrusted, though less and less for younger Moroccans.

"You're never alone, but you can be completely unseen."

This observation comes from a participant in our eight-country investigation of social connection, which conducted in-depth interviews across Brazil, China, India, Morocco, the Philippines, Türkiye, the United States, and Zimbabwe. In earlier posts in this series, we described how loneliness hides behind Brazil's smile, behind Turkish hospitality, behind Filipino cheerfulness, and behind Chinese harmony.

Morocco adds a new chapter to this pattern—and a distinctive mechanism.

We interviewed 50 Moroccans across ages, regions, and loneliness levels, and what they described challenges one of our most stubborn assumptions: that loneliness is a problem of empty rooms and absent people.

In Morocco, the rooms are full. Doors open for unannounced relatives bearing oranges. Neighbors comment on your grocery bags. Extended families gather for Friday couscous, for Eid, for weddings and condolence visits. And yet, within this dense social fabric, some of our participants described a loneliness so profound they compared it to drowning in silence.

When Being Social Is a Moral Test

For many participants, social connection in Morocco is not simply valued, it is moralized. As one young woman put it: "Moroccans don't know the notion of introverts... if you are someone who likes to spend time alone, you will be called autistic, or you have some kind of disease. The more you are socially connected, the more you are seen as a good person."

Another participant framed it as "almost a test of good character... Being sociable is linked to warmth, hospitality, even patriotism. People who prefer quiet are often misunderstood, tagged as strange or aloof. Social connection isn't just valued; it's expected."

The consequence is a distinctive expectation our participants called woujoud fi lwaqt—being present when it counts. Family expects you at weddings and funerals. Friends expect you at 2 a.m. when someone's heartbroken. As one participant summarized: "When you need someone, they show up, and when they need you, you show up. That mutual reliability defines a real connection here."

The Loneliness That Cannot Be Spoken

But this same moral scaffolding makes loneliness nearly impossible to admit. "The unique thing is that Morocco doesn't believe in loneliness," one participant told us. "It's like something out of our jargon... They say, 'You have your health, you eat, you drink, you're good.' It's like you're just victimizing yourself if you're saying that you're lonely."

Another explained the arithmetic of disbelief: "We live packed in big families, so admitting loneliness sounds crazy to others: 'How? House is full!' That makes you hide it more." Admitting loneliness can even sound ungrateful: "You have family, food, a roof. What else do you want?"

The result is concealment. "Some of the loneliest people are great performers," one woman observed. "They laugh, socialize, seem energetic... but when you're close enough, you notice the little things: how fast they change the topic when things get real."

article continues after advertisement

When Couscous Makes It Worse

Perhaps most striking: the very rituals designed to sustain connection can sharpen loneliness for those who already feel unseen. One participant described Fridays—the day of communal couscous and mosque—as her hardest: "Weddings—they amplify the loneliness. The joy in the air makes the silence in your phone feel louder."

Others described attending obligatory gatherings in a state of internal absence—one participant described going on "airplane mode" internally: politely present, entirely disengaged. As one man put it: "You can be surrounded and still feel like nobody sees you. That contrast creates a special kind of quiet pain."

What Connection Actually Means

When we asked Moroccans to define connection, almost no one mentioned how often people meet. Instead, they described a felt quality: "It's when you feel seen. Not just when someone talks to you, but when you speak and they actually hear you." The sample's most isolated participant, an elderly man, reduced it to its essence: "Social connection is someone remembering you exist. Someone calling without needing something."

This is the crucial insight. If connection is defined by being witnessed rather than by contact frequency, then a full house guarantees nothing—and loneliness surveys that count interactions will miss what matters most.

Where Moroccans Turn

Faith emerged as the most consistently genuine source of comfort. "Reading the Qur'an or praying helps me feel connected to God. That eases loneliness," one participant said. Another described prayer as "a reset button, not a hang-out."

Professional help, by contrast, remains distrusted. Among those who tried it, none reported a positive ongoing relationship with a mental health professional. Yet there are signs of change. "Older generations saw loneliness as weakness, or worse, something supernatural—like being masḥūr (cursed)," one young woman noted. "That mindset is shifting. Our generation talks more openly about depression, burnout, isolation."

article continues after advertisement

Across our eight countries, a common thread is emerging: Different peoples develop their own ways of making loneliness invisible. Brazil masks it with a smile, the Philippines with cheerfulness, Türkiye with hospitality, China with harmony. Morocco's version may be the most structural of all: a social world so full, so ritually dense, and so morally committed to togetherness that the lonely have nowhere to stand and say so.

Morocco's lesson for the rest of us is uncomfortable: Abundant social contact is not the cure for loneliness, and mandating togetherness can deepen the wound. What lonely people need is not more rooms full of people. It is one person who notices when their "I'm fine" sounds different.

item.title: Being Creative When You Have No Time
item.description:
Creativity

Being Creative When You Have No Time

Despite how it may feel, creativity doesn’t vanish. Here's how to find and use it.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that creative endeavors reinforce identity, which is crucial for those who care for others.
  • Self-expression is a way to care for the self, and to hold onto oneself while caring for others.
  • Creative pursuits, even for a few minutes per day, can be both grounding and uplifting.

What happens to creativity under real-world pressure?

Many will be interested in the answer, be they caregivers of aging parents or children who are ill (or not), partner caregivers, sandwiched caregivers, paid and unpaid caregivers, and individuals who struggle to be good stewards of their own needs.

The answer? Creativity doesn’t vanish, though it is often disrupted. Caregiving in general is disruptive to creative endeavors, because it constantly interrupts moments of reflection.

"Write every day" was the edict I learned early in my writing at a time I was working in a clinical capacity as well. I understood this to mean that I should expect ideas to bubble up and it was my job to shepherd them into reality—to caretake them, so to speak. But under times of pressure—parenting, illness, stress—writing every day meant spewing emotion into the pages of my journal. Writing every day doesn’t always translate to the kind of creativity—translation: productivity—many desire especially while caring for another.

Caregiving is an exercise in holding a tension. The purity of one’s own ideas exist on one side, and in direct opposition are the imminent needs of someone else. In reality, the two are already co-existing. How can the caregiver gently spin them into a project that is meaningful to them and, perhaps, to others as well?

Alexandra Grabbe was faced with this conundrum in 2006, when her 96-year-old mother became bedridden. During the last year of her mom’s life she postponed a novel. “I simply didn’t have the mental capacity to concentrate for extended periods of time on revision,” she says. “I wrote two blogs, one related to living green on Cape Cod—a promotional effort for my B&B—and the other about home care.” The latter, a chronicle of caring for her mother, originally meant for family updates, began to gain readers who were, in fact, complete strangers. Her writing struck a chord.

At the time she didn’t realize that by writing about her experience she was helping others make sense of their own. Several reached out to thank her. “Since home care of the elderly is such a solitary occupation, it was heartwarming to receive affirmation. “I didn’t stop writing. I simply downsized my ambitions. I looked forward to those delicious moments when I could create,” Grabbe says. One self-avowed “fan” suggested turning her posts into a book, which became Seeing Joy.

Grabbe’s efforts matter. She built a world that allowed her to care for her mother and also for herself, reinforcing her identity as an individual who mattered as much as the mom she adored. This supports the research that has proven the value of creativity for both patients and caregivers to enhance creative discovery and growth, but also to retain and, perhaps, reclaim identity.

article continues after advertisement

Studies repeatedly find that self-expression through art or writing, for example, promotes healthy aging (for children and adolescents it’s referred to as healthy development).

Perhaps it is the act of setting aside time for oneself that is most meaningful. This can be true for a writer, an artist, nature enthusiast, bird watcher, swimmer, walker—whatever brings meaning and value to the individual. As I see it, it’s a delicate balance of self-care, willingness and time—even five minutes a day—that fosters creativity. And those minutes add up, one day at a time.

item.title: Why AI Can’t Be Creative (Yet)
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why AI Can’t Be Creative (Yet)

What happened when I asked Claude to write the most creative sentence in history.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • The more I asked Claude to be creative, the more predictable it became.
  • E. Paul Torrance's creativity research shows fluency and originality are separate things.
  • LLMs predict the most likely words, which is the opposite of originality.
Source: Daniela Paola Alchapar/Unsplash

Last night, I suddenly got an idea. I opened up Claude, the overly-friendly neighborhood AI bot, and asked it: “Hey buddy, write the most creative sentence you possibly could.” Claude almost immediately responded:

“She kept her childhood in a jar of fireflies and opened it only on the nights the dark felt honest.”

Cringe!

Really, Claude? That’s literally the best you can do? So I decided to go even bigger and give it another chance. The biggest, in fact: “You know what, write the most creative sentence ever written in human history!” A few seconds later, Claude responded:

“The universe wrote itself into being one lonely word at a time, and named the ache between the words you.”

Bigger cringe!

How can this be? The second prompt, which was about ALL OF HUMAN HISTORY, was even worse than the first. So this led me down a whole rabbit hole linking this to my lifelong research on the science of creativity and what you get is this 100% human-written post. Let’s go.

The Origins of Creativity Research

Sixty years ago, the creativity researcher E. Paul Torrance was frustrated that the field of psychology was neglecting the study of creativity. Psychology was so focused on IQ (hello Lewis Terman and his obsession with gifted children with high IQs) that barely any researchers found creativity important enough to study. Enter Torrance.

He created his legendary “Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking,” which measures creativity along four major dimensions:

  • Fluency: The sheer quantity of meaningful responses. For example, if the question is “list all the uses for a paperclip,” 30 responses in the span of a few minutes would demonstrate high fluency.
  • Flexibility: The ability to shift categories. For example, a high flexibility score would include uses that cross categories such as office supplies (holding documents together), tools (picking a lock), hygiene (toothpick), and arts/crafts (making a paperclip sculpture).
  • Originality: The statistical rarity of the ideas. Most people would immediately think of “hold paper together,” but an original response would be “bend it into a miniature replica of the Empire State Building.”
  • Elaboration: The depth and detail of the ideas. An example of high elaboration would be something like, “Use it as a plant support system to train and support young seedlings."
article continues after advertisement

Torrance used his tests to follow children from elementary school all the way into adulthood to see how well they predicted creative life outcomes. One follow-up study by Jonathan Plucker found that just under half of the variance in adult creative achievement is explained by his creativity test scores, with the contribution of Torrance’s tests being more than three times that of IQ scores.

Clearly there are deep implications here for human intelligence. But in this post, I want to explore something that isn’t explored nearly enough, and that’s the deep implications for artificial intelligence.

Let’s zoom in on two of the major scoring dimensions: fluency and originality. Torrance’s brilliant observation, which has been empirically supported by many years of creativity research, is that fluency and originality are partially separable aspects of creative thinking. Yes, they are positively correlated with each other, but this isn’t necessarily the case. They are worth measuring separately.

Why AI Tends Toward Predictability When Prompted for Creativity

Now let’s return to Claude’s responses and how it actually got more predictable when I asked it to be more creative. When Claude raised its weights to the maximum of creativity—the most creative sentence in all of human history—Claude went right to the dead center of the archetypical “profound sentence” cluster of its training: the cosmos, loneliness, love, the intimate second-person perspective. To Claude, the deepest thing it could come up with is an assemblage of a million things that have already been labeled deep during the course of human history. So the bigger the demand for originality, the harder the machine regressed to the average of what it thought “genius” is supposed to sound like.

Here’s the incredible irony as I see it: AI just isn’t built for rarity, which is literally the definition of "genius." Turn the creativity dial to maximum and you can pulled as close as possible to the average of “sounds like genius,” but you get something that clearly is not genius.

Now let’s analyze for a moment why neither sentence it gave me is actually creative (and why that’s actually built into the very nature of AI). According to Torrance and modern-day creativity researchers, creativity involves both novelty and meaningfulness. Just originality and you get a word salad. Just meaningfulness with no originality a you get an everyday thought. A sentence is only creative if it says something the way almost nobody else would say it in a way that people (even if it’s only domain experts) can comprehend. But current AI models are built entirely from phrases and images that lots of people already reach for when they’re trying to sound deep or creative.

Take: “She kept her childhood in a jar of fireflies and opened it only on the nights the dark felt honest.”

The idea of putting a memory in a jar is a common convention for creative writers. This is Hallmark Greeting Card common. “Fireflies” are the go-to image for a wistful childhood. We’ve all seen it a thousand times. “The dark felt honest” may on the surface sound meaningful but take a moment and ask yourself: What the hell does that actually mean??! It’s literally a mood pretending to be a thought. The key here is that nothing in this creative attempt could actually be true for any one real human living person. There is no specific memory here, and no real detail. Anyone could have written it.

article continues after advertisement

Why Human Writing Remains Unique and Irreplaceable

I want to end this article on a note that illustrates why current AI models will not be taking over human writing anytime soon. Here’s the thing: What I am writing right now at this very moment comes from MY heart. Not the average heart of human history, but my heart.

The thing that makes human writing so special is that we can write from a real lived human experience and we can choose to deliberately create sentences and use word choices that are infinitely original and interesting. AI models in their current LLM instantiation are built to not be capable of doing that because statistical rarity is the opposite of what it’s grasping for when it composes sentences.***

Interestingly enough, the way AI detectors work is by analyzing how much a certain chunk of text is predictable. Because that’s all AI knows how to write. Just for kicks, I went onto Pangram and put this Claude-generated text in there:

“She kept her childhood in a jar of fireflies and opened it only on the nights the dark felt honest. The universe wrote itself into being one lonely word at a time, and named the ache between the words you. Grief moved into the guest room and paid rent in small forgettings.”

It came back: “100% of this text is AI.” I then replaced it with a paragraph from this very article, and it came back: “100% of this text is Human Written.”

Isn’t that interesting? I don’t think the value of human writing is going away anytime soon. I, for one, am going to stick to my own soul revealing itself on the paper. Not only does that feel more fun and meaningful, but I also bet that sentence right there is probably actually more creative than any other sentence ever written in human history (according to Claude).

item.title: What Jimothy the Raccoon Reveals About Our Need for Nature
item.description:
Environment

What Jimothy the Raccoon Reveals About Our Need for Nature

Why one wild raccoon captivated millions—and what it says about us.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Something essential is lost when our lives become human-centric.
  • Animals like Jimothy helps us to recognize that we have become disconnected from the natural world.
  • Collective effervescence can create bonding through the shared experiences of joy, wonder, or awe.
  • Jimothy helps us to remember that we are a part of the bigger ecosystem around us.
Source: Toan Chu via Unsplash

A Seattle-area raccoon with a shortened spine has become one of the internet's most celebrated animals. Videos of Jimothy waddling through neighborhoods, balancing on backyard fences, and going about his nightly routine have gained millions of views. His popularity makes sense: He’s endearing and easy to recognize with his unique body shape. But what if our emotional investment in the life of a wild raccoon had less to do with Jimothy himself and more to do with what he awakens inside of us?

From Human-Centric to Wild Otherness

Modern life has become almost entirely human-centric. We spend our days in environments shaped entirely for people, created by people. Our screens and daily lives mostly reflect us to ourselves. Ecophilosopher David Abrams argues that something essential is lost when our lives become human-centric. People are wired to interact with what he calls wild otherness: non-human living beings whose lives contrast our own. Encounters with wild animals de-center humans in a way that is both fascinating and expansive. Jimothy’s presence pulls us out of our own world and reminds us that we are fellow creatures existing within an ecosystem, in relationship with our environment.

We Are Missing a Sense of Belonging to the Living World

Perhaps what draws us to Jimothy is not only his intriguing way of navigating urban life as a uniquely shaped raccoon, but the recognition that we ourselves have become disconnected from the natural world in the digital age. Seeing videos of him reminds us of this long-lost part of ourselves: the child who delighted in exploring nature with wonder and curiosity, living within a simpler world. Environmental psychology uses the term ecological identity to describe the part of our personal identities that is formed through relationships with landscapes, plants, and animals, which offer a psychological sense of belonging to the larger community of life that shapes value systems (Clayton). Recognizing that our identities extend beyond the borders of our skin and psyche to include the natural world around us helps us to experience a sense of belonging. Our conscious awareness of our neighborhoods shifts from houses to ecosystems. Families of birds live in the trees, their lives unfolding in parallel with our own. We exist as members of a larger web of life.

article continues after advertisement
Jimothy runs across the sidewalk.
Source: Kiana Hall. Used with permission

We Benefit From Shared Wonder

In a hyperconnected world, it’s easy to become overwhelmed by the constant stream of political conflicts, climate anxiety, and stories of loneliness, leaving little room for the emotions of joy and wonder. And yet, millions paused to take wonder in the same unlikely creature. Collective effervescence is the term used to describe shared experiences of joy, wonder, or awe that can strengthen social bonds. Jimothy brought people together to smile at the same unlikely creature.

What Jimothy Really Represents

Jimothy is adored not only for who he is, but also for what he represents to us. He reminds us that we, as humans, are not the center of the world. Jimothy draws us out of our own concerns and stressors to remember that we are a part of the bigger ecosystem around us, and that we were built for relationships beyond just those with other humans. Sometimes it just takes a uniquely shaped raccoon to help us remember that we’ve belonged to nature all along.

item.title: Are We Testing for Drugs—or Trust?
item.description:
Addiction

Are We Testing for Drugs—or Trust?

When mandatory drug screening becomes a barrier to outpatient addiction care.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Stigma remains a major barrier to accessing addiction treatment.
  • Mandatory drug testing may unintentionally reinforce stigma.
  • A collaborative approach can preserve accountability while honoring dignity and self-determination.

After years of working in outpatient behavioral health programs, I have seen drug screens function as useful clinical tools. I have also seen them become moments of embarrassment, defensiveness, shame, and rupture.

This is the tension I want to name carefully: Drug testing is not inherently harmful. In some cases, it can support safety, guide medication decisions, help assess risk, or provide accountability for someone who wants external structure. But mandatory drug screening for voluntary outpatient participants raises a deeper psychological question.

Is the practice always congruent with what we now know about trauma, motivation, stigma, and recovery?

In many ways, therapeutic culture has evolved faster than some of our institutional practices. We speak the language of person-centered care, trauma-informed treatment, harm reduction, cultural humility, and dignity. Yet some policies still carry the older grammar of surveillance, compliance, and mistrust.

Stigma Keeps People From Seeking Care

Addiction remains one of the most stigmatized health conditions in the United States. Although neuroscience has helped reframe addiction as a complex medical and behavioral health condition, many people who struggle with substance use disorders are still met with judgment, suspicion, and shame.

This stigma is not merely painful. It can become a barrier to care. In 2021, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) estimated that 46 million Americans met criteria for a substance use disorder, while only 6 percent received treatment. That gap should concern anyone working in behavioral health.

When people expect to be shamed, blamed, or punished, they may delay asking for help until consequences become more severe. Patients may internalize stigma, and treatment systems can unintentionally reproduce it.

That is why outpatient practices deserve careful reflection. A policy may be designed to support recovery, yet still communicate something psychologically damaging.

The Clinical Case for Drug Screening

There are legitimate reasons outpatient programs use drug screening. Tests can provide information that self-report alone may not capture. They may help clinicians identify risk, adjust treatment planning, or make safer medication decisions. For patients involved with courts, employers, or licensing boards, documentation of abstinence may be part of what allows them to return to work, family, or community responsibilities.

For some people, drug testing can even feel supportive. A patient may say, “I want the accountability,” or “Seeing the results motivates me.” In those cases, screening can become part of a recovery structure that the person actively chooses.

Yet there are concerns about differential treatment. Many kinds of information would be clinically useful in other areas of medicine, but patients are not usually required to prove compliance through mandatory bodily fluid testing as a condition of voluntary outpatient care. When people with substance use disorders are singled out in this way, the practice can unintentionally reinforce the assumption that they are less trustworthy than other patients.

The problem is not the existence of drug screening. The problem is when it becomes the central measure of recovery, when it is imposed in ways that weaken trust, or when it treats people with substance use disorders differently from patients managing other complex health conditions.

The Therapeutic Alliance Is Treatment

article continues after advertisement

In outpatient care, the therapeutic relationship is not just the container for treatment. It is part of the treatment.

If trust is central to healing, we have to ask what is communicated when a person voluntarily enters care and is told, in effect, “We need proof that you are telling the truth.”

For patients who already carry shame about addiction, this can be a powerful message. Even when clinicians do not intend mistrust, the system may still imply it. A urine screen can begin to feel less like a lab test and more like a moral one.

This is especially important because many people with substance use disorders have histories of trauma. Trauma-informed care emphasizes safety, trustworthiness, collaboration, empowerment, voice, and choice. Mandatory screening may work against those principles when it is experienced as coercive, humiliating, or punitive.

Words Matter

Important efforts have been made across behavioral health to move away from pejorative labels such as “addict” or “alcoholic,” especially when those terms reduce a whole person to a diagnosis or behavior. The language around drug testing also matters.

A “clean” or “dirty drop" is not neutral language. It turns a clinical data point into a moral symbol. If a patient has reduced use, improved relationships, returned to work or meaningful activities, stabilized housing, or begun participating sincerely in therapy, a positive urine screen may still be treated as failure.

But recovery is rarely linear.

A positive screen does not reveal much about a person’s lived experience nor their full metabolic condition. In my own clinical experience, I have also been involved with false positives and mislabeled samples that led to significant therapeutic ruptures, reminding me that even “objective” data is not always objective.

When treatment becomes organized around pass or fail, clean or dirty, compliant or noncompliant, we risk flattening recovery into a false binary.

Surveillance Is Not Experienced Equally

Drug policy has never been applied equally. Poor and marginalized communities have often experienced substance use disorders less as a health issue and more as a criminalized identity. In healthcare, mandatory drug screening can echo that larger history, especially when patients have little real choice about whether to comply.

article continues after advertisement

Who is believed? Who is monitored? Who receives flexibility? Who is discharged? Who gets another chance?

I have participated in very serious interdisciplinary debates in staff meetings when there is not policy consistency in abstinence-only group programs. These questions shape whether people feel safe and equal enough to be open.

Accountability Without Shame

Motivation is often strengthened by autonomy, competence, and connection. Yet many treatment systems still rely heavily on external control.

Accountability does not have to mean surveillance. A more therapeutic approach would begin with conversation. A social worker might ask: “Would drug screening help support your recovery goals?” For one person, the answer may be yes. They may want regular testing as structure, motivation, or evidence of change. For another person, especially someone with a history of coercion, institutional mistrust, or shame, mandatory testing may increase defensiveness and reduce transparency.

In that case, other tools may be more useful: self-reporting, motivational interviewing, clinical assessment, peer support, harm-reduction planning, medication management, family work, or more frequent therapeutic check-ins.

This does not mean abandoning structure but humanizing it.

The Deeper Issue Is Dignity

Drug screening can be reframed as one possible tool within a comprehensive care plan, not the central measure of recovery. When used, it should be explained clearly, consented to meaningfully, interpreted carefully, and discussed without shame.

A positive test should open a clinical conversation, not automatically trigger punishment or discharge: What happened? What was the context? What support was missing? What can be adjusted? What does the patient want to understand about the data?

article continues after advertisement

These questions preserve dignity while still taking substance use seriously.

If addiction treatment is to move beyond the moralistic assumptions of the past, our practices must evolve too. We cannot say addiction is a health condition while treating people as though they are primarily dishonest, dangerous, or defective. We cannot claim to be trauma-informed while ignoring how surveillance may feel to those whose lives have already been shaped by powerlessness.

Recovery is not only measured by what disappears from a toxicology report, but by what reappears in a person’s life.

A more ethical path is collaborative accountability: care that respects autonomy, acknowledges structural inequities, and treats each person not as a problem to monitor, but as the expert of their own life.

item.title: When Life Gives You Lemons, Pull Over
item.description:
Mindfulness

When Life Gives You Lemons, Pull Over

If we go too fast, summer will do the same.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • It's hard to appreciate surprises along the way when we're going so fast.
  • We take time to work, but what about play?
  • Summer—and life—are fleeting; slowing down lets us truly experience them.
Summer doesn't wait forever.
Source: Alicja Gancarz/Unsplash

Not far from home, on a grassy perch at the intersection of a neighborhood drive and a busy road, the two girls wait. It’s hard not to notice them sitting there under a tree with their table and makeshift sign, jumping up and waving each time a car goes by. Slow down, they say. Take a break. Buy some lemonade.

But, of course, most cars whiz by, the drivers on their way to work or errands or whatever busyness the day requires. Doesn’t matter that the sky is cloudless and the humidity finally washed away with last night’s shower, leaving a pleasant breeze in its place. Doesn’t matter that the young entrepreneurs are hopeful and the drinks they’re selling are homemade. Doesn’t matter that the price amounts to little more than spare change and the diversion will only take a moment, maybe two.

Slow down, they say. Take a break. Buy some lemonade.

Why People Pass by Opportunities to Pause

Apparently, what matters more to the passersby is keeping to schedule, not stopping, not losing time.

Besides, the girls will be there again. Just like the beaches will be waiting, the water will be warm. The tennis courts will be open, as will the golf courses. There will be plenty of time for moonlit walks, dinners with friends, afternoons on the porch wrapped up in a book. They will all be there, waiting like the girls for us, whenever we’re ready, whenever we can take a break, whenever we stop driving, driving, driving.

By the way, the reason I know about the girls on the side of the road is because I, too, have driven by them. Not once. Not twice. OK. Many, many times. And each time, there was this feeling in the pit of my stomach, deep and gnawing, that I was going too fast, passing by too quickly, missing a chance that might not come again. Yet, despite it, I’m sad to admit I kept to my schedule. I didn’t stop. I didn’t lose time.

Lose time. How do you do that, I wonder? I mean, really. Time is a gift we receive the second we’re born, a shiny piggy bank filled with all of our moments, our days, our years. Only trouble is, we can’t see into our bank, we can’t crack it open and spill out its contents, and so we’ve got no way of knowing how much is in there. How much we’ve got. How much we’ve got left. There’s no way to save it or store it or deposit more minutes to replenish the ones we’ve already gone through.

All we can do is spend our time. Carefully. Thoughtfully. Consciously. And appreciate our moments along the way.

Does Speeding Up Make Time Go Faster?

If we go faster and faster, does time speed up to keep pace or does it just seem that way? And if we slow down, might time return the favor?

From the window in my office, I can see the sky, cerulean and cloudless. There’s a breeze, too, fresh and inviting, stirring up some papers on my desk and some thoughts in my head.

article continues after advertisement

There are so many things I’ve been meaning to do before the summer ends. And it will. Too soon. Too fleeting. There’s a friend who wants to go for a walk along the rocky shore, another who’s hoping we can play tennis. There’s a great café with outdoor seating where I’ve been meaning to take my husband for breakfast. I haven’t been on the bike trail in a long time or watched the sun slip into the horizon beyond the beach. They just started serving pistachio soft serve at my favorite ice-cream stand.

And yes, I know a great place to stop for lemonade.
